sections.title: Euler’s Totient Theorem for Remainders
sections.content: If a and n are co-prime, then a^phi(n) ≡ 1 (mod n). Steps: (1) Check whether gcd(a, n) = 1. (2) Compute phi(n) using prime factorization of n. (3) Reduce the exponent modulo phi(n). (4) Rewrite the expression using the reduced exponent. (5) Evaluate the smaller power. This method is useful for large exponential remainder problems.

sections.title: Fermat’s Little Theorem Applications
sections.content: If p is prime and p does not divide a, then a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Steps: (1) Identify that modulus is prime. (2) Confirm a is not divisible by p. (3) Reduce exponent modulo (p-1). (4) Rewrite expression accordingly. (5) Compute simplified remainder. This is highly effective for competitive exams.

sections.title: Wilson’s Theorem in Factorial Remainders
sections.content: For a prime p, (p-1)! ≡ -1 (mod p). Steps: (1) Confirm p is prime. (2) Express factorial in terms of (p-1)!. (3) Replace using theorem. (4) Adjust sign under modulus. (5) Simplify final remainder. Useful in factorial-based remainder problems.

sections.title: Finding Last Two Digits Using Cyclic Patterns
sections.content: To find last two digits, work modulo 100. Steps: (1) Reduce base modulo 100. (2) Identify cyclicity pattern of powers. (3) Reduce exponent using cycle length. (4) Compute reduced power. (5) Extract final two digits. Especially important for numbers ending in 1, 3, 7, 9.

sections.title: Highest Power of a Prime in Factorial
sections.content: Exponent of prime p in n! equals floor(n/p) + floor(n/p^2) + floor(n/p^3) ... until quotient becomes zero. Steps: (1) Divide n by p. (2) Take integer part. (3) Divide by higher powers. (4) Add all integer quotients. (5) Conclude exponent. This also helps in finding trailing zeros.

sections.title: Advanced LCM-Based Remainder Model
sections.content: If a number leaves remainders r1, r2, r3 when divided by m1, m2, m3 respectively and (m1 - r1) = (m2 - r2) = (m3 - r3), then N + k is LCM(m1, m2, m3). Steps: (1) Check common difference. (2) Compute LCM. (3) Subtract common value. (4) Verify conditions. (5) State final answer.

sections.title: Successive Division and Absolute Number Formation
sections.content: If a number when divided successively by m and n leaves remainders r1 and r2, then number = m × (n × q + r2) + r1. Steps: (1) Start from final remainder. (2) Multiply by previous divisor. (3) Add previous remainder. (4) Continue backward if needed. (5) Simplify expression.

problem_frameworks.title: Multi-Theorem Remainder Strategy
problem_frameworks.description: Combine Fermat/Euler reduction with cyclic pattern recognition.
problem_frameworks.steps: Check co-prime condition → apply theorem → reduce exponent → analyze cycle → compute remainder.

problem_frameworks.title: Factorial and Divisibility Integration
problem_frameworks.description: Integrate factorial exponent logic with remainder reasoning.
problem_frameworks.steps: Prime analysis → exponent calculation → compare required power → simplify → conclude.

problem_frameworks.title: LCM and Modular Reconstruction Model
problem_frameworks.description: Reconstruct unknown number using LCM and congruence adjustment.
problem_frameworks.steps: Identify pattern → compute LCM → adjust constant → verify divisibility → finalize.
